nh4no3-solid.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid ammonium nitrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed

note.value:
The ammonium nitrate on this bench is about 4 g of the solid, dissolved in 50.0 mL of water, about 1 mol/L. The supplier's sheet for the solid keeps it from heat, anything that burns, strong acids and powdered metals; it is not ground, and its dust is not breathed. Its sheet for the solution at this strength prints no signal word and no hazard statement. Both call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record marks it as explosive as well as a strong oxidising agent, and says that clothing it gets on can be a fire risk once dry; a second supplier's sheet has such clothing taken off and washed, and asks, for the eyes, flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

aluminium-piece.classifiedAs: Hazards of aluminium metal, the solid and not its powder or dust, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The aluminium on this bench is a solid piece, not a powder, heated in boiling water on purpose. The supplier's sheet for aluminium prints no signal word and no hazard statement. Its dust burns, it says, its powder heats with water, and acids free hydrogen. It calls for eye and face protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet, for shot, adds strong alkalis, so the piece is kept from this lab's acid and base. It lists water and too much heat as well, but of water says that it is the molten metal that reacts. For the eyes it asks 15 minutes or more of flushing and a doctor at once. NOAA's record has the powder react with water and catch fire in air: the powder is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

iron-piece.classifiedAs: Hazards of iron metal, in bulk pieces, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The iron on this bench is a solid piece, not filings or powder, heated in boiling water on purpose. The supplier's sheet for iron in bulk pieces prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It keeps the metal from acids and moisture. It names nothing to be worn, but says to keep the metal from the eyes and to wash the hands.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a metal maker's sheet for iron pieces asks for safety glasses and, for the eyes, 15 minutes or more of flushing; two suppliers' sheets for filings add gloves, protective clothing and a doctor, one of them at once. One classes fine filings as a flammable solid, and NOAA's record has the powder catching fire in air: filings and powder are another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

zinc-piece.classifiedAs: Hazards of zinc metal, as shot, sheet, foil or granules, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The zinc here is a solid piece, not dust, heated in boiling water on purpose. The supplier's sheet for zinc shot, sheet and foil prints no signal word or hazard statement, puts fire hazards with the dust, and keeps it from strong acids and bases. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet, for shot, adds water, from which zinc may free hydrogen, and too much heat. It says zinc may cause dermatitis and rub eyes sore, and for the eyes asks 15 minutes or more of flushing and a doctor at once. A third's calls zinc very toxic to water life: it is kept out of drains and waterways. By NOAA's record zinc dust and damp ammonium nitrate react violently: the two are kept apart.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

tin-piece.classifiedAs: Hazards of tin metal, as shot, granules, mossy pieces or foil, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The tin on this bench is a solid piece, not a powder, heated in boiling water on purpose. The supplier's sheet for tin as shot, granules or foil prints no signal word and no hazard statement, and says that finely divided tin may burn. It keeps tin from halogens, sulfur, and strong bases and oxidisers. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet, for shot, adds acids, which free hydrogen from it, as a third's does: the piece is kept from this lab's acid. The second has tin irritate the eyes, NOAA's record the skin and airways too; for the eyes the second asks 15 minutes or more of flushing and a doctor at once. By NOAA's record the powder, unlike the solid, corrodes in air.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.
